title: Should sport be funded from public money?

turns.speaker: Yara
turns.text: The elite programme's had its funding renewed and the community pools are still closing. Same department, same budget line.

turns.speaker: Steph
turns.text: Because medals are countable and a swimming lesson isn't.

turns.speaker: Ronan
turns.text: That's not entirely fair. The argument is that medals inspire participation, and if that worked it would justify itself.

turns.speaker: Yara
turns.text: Except it's been measured repeatedly and the effect is small and short. A few weeks after a games, and then back.

turns.speaker: Ronan
turns.text: Small and short, or hard to measure? Those aren't the same.

turns.speaker: Yara
turns.text: Fair challenge. But the countries with the highest adult participation aren't the ones topping medal tables. They're the ones with a pool within a mile.

turns.speaker: Steph
turns.text: Which is the whole argument in one sentence.

turns.speaker: Steph
turns.text: Facilities beat inspiration. You can't be inspired into a building that closed.

turns.speaker: Ronan
turns.text: I'd still defend some elite funding. There's a national thing that isn't about participation at all, and pretending it's only instrumental is dishonest.

turns.speaker: Yara
turns.text: Then argue for it on those grounds, rather than on a participation claim that doesn't hold.

turns.speaker: Steph
turns.text: The health case for the pools is the strongest thing on the table and it's the one nobody makes, because the savings land on a different department.

turns.speaker: Yara
turns.text: Ten years later, and after the person who closed it has moved on.

points: Elite sport funding was renewed while community pools close from the same budget.
Ronan presents the standard justification, that medals inspire participation.
Yara says measured inspiration effects are small and short-lived, lasting weeks after a games.
She adds that countries with the highest adult participation have local facilities rather than the most medals.
Ronan concedes the participation argument but defends elite funding on national rather than instrumental grounds, which Yara accepts as the honest case.
Steph argues the health savings from community pools are the strongest argument and go unmade because they accrue to another department years later.
